findings.title: SQL injection via unvalidated sort column
findings.description: The `sort` parameter is directly interpolated into the SQL string with an f-string (`f" ORDER BY {sort} DESC"`) without any allowlist validation or escaping. Since `search_expenses` takes `sort` as a caller-controlled argument, if it is ever derived from user input (e.g., an API query parameter for sorting search results), an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL (e.g., `sort="id; DROP TABLE expenses;--"` or a UNION-based injection to exfiltrate other users' data), unlike the `params` list used for `user_id`/`text` which are safely parameterized.

findings.title: No pagination/limit on search results
findings.description: Unlike the adjacent function which applies `LIMIT ? OFFSET ?` with `PAGE_SIZE`, `search_expenses` has no limit at all. A broad search term (e.g., a common substring) against a large expenses table could return an unbounded number of rows, causing excessive memory use and slow responses.

findings.title: LIKE wildcard characters in search text are not escaped
findings.description: `text` is inserted into the LIKE pattern (`f"%{text}%"`) without escaping `%` or `_`, so if a user's note-search text itself contains these characters, they will be interpreted as SQL wildcards rather than literal characters, producing incorrect/surprising search results.

findings.title: No tests added for new function
findings.description: The PR adds `search_expenses` but includes no unit tests covering basic search behavior, the `sort` parameter, empty/no-match results, or (critically) the SQL-injection risk from the unvalidated `sort` argument.
